<reason>B built the debate around a concrete, transparently-labeled numerical model (100 contacts, $5 vs $0.10, stress-tested against CON's own worst-case escalation rate) and repeatedly forced A to name a flip-point, which A never did — instead retreating to an unquantified "unbounded, correlated risk" framing. That framing is conceptually interesting (tail risk vs. additive cost) and A used it skillfully in the governance-cost and Klarna rebuttals, and A's closing catch on B's "every failure path ends at a human" was a genuinely sharp point. But under the motion's explicit "comparison of magnitudes" framing, refusing twice to engage with any threshold or quantity, while the opponent offers a stress-tested (if illustrative) model, is a real execution cost. B also neutralized A's core "invisible harm" move by pointing out silent churn/abandonment exists in the human baseline too, and turned the accountability argument (audit trail, single-patch correction) into an asset rather than a liability more persuasively than A's rebuttal that identical errors scale before detection. Overall B made the clash easier to adjudicate and pressed harder on the decisive burden; A's case, while intelligent, stayed more abstract and evasive on the actual comparison the motion demands.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's arithmetic model in Rebuttal 1 (B2.1-B2.3), stress-tested again in Rebuttal 2 after Pressure Questions, combined with the repeated "name the flip-rate" challenge that A never answered with a number — this was the single most decisive, unresolved pressure point in the debate.</best_rebuttal>
